Racial Hypocrisy and the Chagos Islands

Forty-four years ago, the Royal Navy sailed thousands of miles across the sea to defend a small archipelago of islands in the South Atlantic, following Argentina’s invasion of British-administered territory, the Falkland Islands. Earlier this year, I saw hundreds of Chagossian people outside the Royal Courts of Justice protesting for another small archipelago of islands. This archipelago, unlike the Falklands whose sovereignty Britain continues to assert, is the subject of a sovereignty dispute with Mauritius. Although the UK and Mauritius signed an agreement in May 2025 providing for the transfer of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago to Mauritius, the agreement has not entered into force. Yet, as James Cartlidge puts it, His Majesty’s Government would be surrendering British claims to the territory not “because of military defeat, or because of a binding legal verdict, but wilfully due to a total failure to take a stand and fight for Britain’s interests on the world stage—a complete and utter negotiating failure” (Cartlidge, 2025). However, the key question that arises for me isn’t a fear of defence or the economic effects upon Britain but this: if self-determination is a universal principle rather than one applied selectively according to the race, geography or political significance of a population, why should the wishes of the Chagossians themselves not be central to determining the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands? The issue, therefore, extends further than a mere territorial dispute. It raises the question of whether the political agency of a displaced people is afforded the same consideration as that of a nation whose continued presence on its territory has become central to a sovereignty dispute.

The constant discourse surrounding the Falklands is that “The British Government has been consistent in its view that the future of the Falklands can only be determined by the people who live there”, and that the sovereignty of British territory cannot pass hands without referendum (Hague 2012). In 2013, a referendum was held to answer the determination question in the Falklands, as “Only the Falkland Islands people can determine how they wish to be governed” (Browne 2012). This establishes a clear position on the relationship between sovereignty and self-determination: the wishes of the population concerned are treated as necessary to determining its future. However, the legitimacy of this becomes difficult to assess when applied to the Chagos Archipelago, because the distinction between the two populations is convoluted by the forced displacement of the Chagossians. The Chagossians no longer inhabit the Chagos Archipelago, as their ancestors did, due to their expulsion between 1968 and 1973, in order to make the British Indian Ocean Territories “available for the establishment of a joint UK-US military base on the largest of the islands, Diego Garcia” (BIOT 2019). There appears to be a fundamental injustice in allowing the consequences of a population's forced removal to complicate the recognition of its political wishes, especially when the removal itself was carried out by the same state now negotiating the territory's future.

That said, a statement delivered to the UN Conference on Trade and Development by HE Mark Matthews, Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations for the UK in relation to the sovereignty of the Falklands stated that:

The British Government also has no doubt about its sovereignty of the Chagos Archipelago which it administers as the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT). No international tribunal, including the Arbitral Tribunal constituted under Annex VII to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), has ever called the UK’s sovereignty of the Territory into doubt. (Matthews 2016)

Although the legal circumstances of the two archipelagos differ, the question of consistency remains. If Britain consider the wishes of the inhabitants of the Falklands fundamental to determining their political future, it must provide a valid explanation of why the position of the Chagossians should carry less weight. This does not necessarily mean that both populations possess identical legal rights, however it raises questions about Britain’s consistency in their application of the principle of self-determination.

This is not an argument suggesting Britain was innocent in the history of the Chagos Archipelago, but quite the contrary, the forced displacement of the Chagossians is the reason why their political rights deserve utmost consideration. Conversely, the issue isn’t as simple as declaring the islands as British sovereign territory. In its 2019 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice concluded that:

The process of decolonization of Mauritius was not lawfully completed in 1968, the Court examined the consequences, under international law, arising from the United Kingdom’s continued administration of the Chagos Archipelago. In particular, it was of the opinion that the United Kingdom’s continued administration of the Chagos Archipelago “constitutes a wrongful act entailing the international responsibility of that State”, that the United Kingdom “has an obligation to bring to an end its administration of the Chagos Archipelago as rapidly as possible, and that all Member States must co-operate with the United Nations to complete the decolonization of Mauritius” (ICJ 2019)

The real question that remains is whether the right to self-determination belongs exclusively to the former colony of Mauritius or does it belong to the Chagossians as a distinct group belonging to the Archipelago. As Stephen Allen discusses, resolving the question of Mauritian sovereignty does not resolve the separate issue of how Chagossian self-determination should be recognised, raisin an important distinction between territorial sovereignty and the political autonomy of a displaced group (Allen, 2020).

The distinction is important as if the Chagossians constitute a separate “people” displaced by colonialism then under the UN’s The Right to Self Determination the Chagossians have right to self-determination. In the document it states that in the right to self-determination in the anti-colonial struggle, “We reaffirm the inalienable right of all colonial peoples to self-determination, freedom and independence and condemn all actions which deprive any people of these rights” (UN 1981). Yet, if the relevant people for the purposes of international law are the people of Mauritius as a whole, then the Chagossians' position may not give them a veto over the territorial settlement. The dispute therefore cannot be reduced to a simple contest between British and Mauritian sovereignty. It now becomes a dispute over who has the right to decide. The significance of this dispute is not merely theoretical either: the Chagossians themselves have expressed “a clear wish for greater Chagossian agency in future decisions made about the islands,” making it clear that the claim is not a dispute between two nations disputing sovereignty over an archipelago, but detrimental to people whose lives, history, and identity are woven into the Chagos Islands (House of Lords 2025). Furthermore, if the purpose of returning the islands is one of decolonisation, as the UN affirms, why should the islands be ‘returned’ to Mauritius when a survey of three thousand Chagossians articulated distrust of the Mauritian government, fearing a lack of safeguarding rooted in historical marginalisation and discrimination against the Chagossian people? (UK Parliament 2025).

This is where Britain’s position on the Falklands becomes crucial. If self-determination is a universal principle, it cannot solely be applied when it suits British interests. The displacement of the Chagossians by the British makes their exclusion from decisions of their homeland particularly troubling. Although the legal situation of the Falklands and Chagos differ, those differences should not make Chagossian political agency irrelevant to the archipelago’s future. This contrast therefore raises a wider question of whether Britain’s commitment to self-determination is applied consistently, or whether the political wishes of some populations are met with greater consideration than others. If the decision of the Falkland Islanders can be treated as a decisive consideration in determining sovereignty, then the wishes of Chagossians deserve at least equal consideration. If the purpose of decolonisation is to give people autonomy and the right to determine their own future, the Chagossians must be meaningfully involved in decisions that recognise their homeland. Otherwise, Britain risks defending self-determination as a principle when it serves British interests while neglecting it when it does not.
